title: Let them come
hook: Jews sit shiva; some Muslim families receive mourners for three days: grief is meant to be accompanied

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Kristin Neff, and her self-compassion break. Your line was others feel this too.

A casserole dish on a doorstep, covered in foil, with a note taped to the lid. By evening there's another. Then a bag of bagels, a tray of fruit, somebody's aunt at the door with a pot of soup. On some streets, when there's been a death, the food starts arriving before anyone asks for it. And for the family inside, the hard part may not be cooking at all. It's opening the door. In more than one tradition, grief is meant to have company, not a quiet house.
screen: `A DISH ON THE DOORSTEP.` → `THE HARD PART: OPENING THE DOOR.` → `GRIEF IS MEANT TO HAVE COMPANY.`

segments.voice: First, the seven days. In Jewish tradition, after a burial, the close family sits shiva. They stay home, and the community comes to them. The Bible already knows a seven-day mourning: when Jacob dies, Genesis says of his son Joseph, "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Some families leave the front door unlocked during shiva, so visitors can let themselves in and the mourners don't have to get up. Second, the first meal. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, says the first meal after the burial should come from someone else's hands, not the mourner's own kitchen. Neighbors cook. The mourner's job is to eat. Third, the same instinct in another house. A hadith tells of the day news came that a man named Ja'far had died. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told the people to prepare food for Ja'far's family, because something had come to them that would keep them busy. It's in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. In some Muslim families today, relatives and neighbors receive visitors and bring meals for three days. Fourth, the other side of the door. Every one of these customs needs two people. Someone carries the soup up the path. Someone else has to open the door and take it. For a person who is used to being the helper, that second job can feel like the harder one. In these traditions, saying yes to the casserole isn't a failure at grieving. It is part of how grieving is done. The visitors come. The mourner lets them.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AT HOME.` · `THE FIRST MEAL FROM OTHER HANDS.` · `FOOD FOR JA'FAR'S FAMILY.` · `SOMEONE HAS TO OPEN THE DOOR.` · then, large: `LET THEM COME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has offered help you waved away, or someone who would come if you asked. Let the door open in your mind, let them stand there with whatever they're carrying, and notice what happens when you imagine saying yes; if something tightens, breathe there. If you pray, you can bring that person to God by name, and then simply breathe, as someone who is allowed to be cared for.
Shiva, the week a Jewish family sits at home after a burial while the community comes to them. Today's word.
Your line: someone else's hands. Even a small yes, a ride or a coffee, counts. That's day seven hundred forty-three.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): Genesis 50:10 KJV checked exact; Moed Katan 27b (mourner may not eat his own bread at the first meal), Abu Dawud 3132 and Tirmidhi 998 (food for Ja'far's family) match. No change.

Jewish Keeper: please check the description of shiva (family at home, community visits), the unlocked-door custom (stated as 'some families'), and the attribution of the meal of condolence (seudat havra'ah) to Moed Katan 27b.
Original game: שִׁבְעָה glossed as 'the word for seven'; please confirm the pointing and the pronunciation 'shiv-AH' (colloquially SHIV-uh).

Islam Keeper: the Ja'far hadith is paraphrased (Abu Dawud 3132, Tirmidhi 998); please confirm numbering. The script deliberately does not state Ja'far's relationship to the Prophet or how he died, since the hadith text cited does not say so.

The index hook says 'many Muslims receive mourners for three'; softened to 'some Muslim families' under the claims rule. Bukhari 1280 is listed as background for the three-day limit on mourning; scholars differ on how it relates to the custom of receiving condolences, so the script does not link them explicitly.
The index hook says 'Jews sit shiva for seven days'; the script says the family sits shiva and grounds 'seven days' in Genesis 50:10 rather than stating a rule of practice.
